lines: If I might explain this succinctly, the critical message from the film, "Indonesia Calling", is, firstly, self-determination is the right of every nation. And this was a new concept when Indonesia proclaimed independence. So you have to think back to that time when Indonesia seized that tiny window of opportunity.

Japan was defeated, the Allies were yet to arrive, and Indonesia proclaimed independence. It was quite a bold and strategic move, right? And the world just wasn’t ready for it. With that in mind, you must take note that the Dutch and the Allies were victorious in World War 2 but they did not anticipate Sukarno’s proclamation of independence.

It was a good few months before they retaliated in response because they didn’t see it coming. As I said before, the primary message of this film is that independence is the right of every nation and that was an emerging notion. The second important message of this film, in my opinion, is that the sovereignty of each nation is the business of all nations.

Indonesia did not achieve independence by her own efforts alone. You could just go and make a speech just like the People’s Democratic Party activists did proclaiming independence. But if you did it in front of a microphone like this, you’d be beaten up by the military. You can imagine what it was like back then.

In the streets and markets of Indonesia there were declarations of independence, but Indonesia had yet printed its own currency. The Rupiah didn’t yet exist. It was still Dutch and Japanese money. So it was really nothing more than a speech, “Independence”, and it was precarious, very fragile.

Because of that, Indonesia’s independence could have very easily been thwarted by the Allies who had successfully defeated Japan. However, as I said, the notion of independence being the right of every nation, that’s an international concept, a global concept, not a notion confined to individual countries.

For that very reason, Australia, India and China expressed their support for Indonesia. This is the second critical message. I’d like to take the opportunity this morning to contemplate with you all, what do those two key ideas mean to contemporary Indonesia? I’ll start by saying that Indonesia today is so very different to Indonesia seventy odd years ago.

The notion of nationalism, of the right to self-determination, is vastly different to what is was back then. And how is it different? Our conception has narrowed. And that’s why I think this film is so important to remind of us of that, to expand our thinking, about what it means to be a nation.

In Indonesia, there are two prominent ideologies currently at conflict, of the many ideologies and concepts at play in Indonesia that are quite complex. From all of these ideologies, there are two that are currently predominant and at odds with each other. The first, of course, is nationalism, a concept that is quite serious and fiercely defended by its proponents.

This concept conflicts with another significant ideology. To put it simply, this ideology is derived from Islam. These days, you can read the newspapers anywhere and see “Indonesia does not subscribe to radicalism or terrorism”. I think this assertion stems from the conflict between these two ideologies.

This morning, I’m not here to talk about Islam but, rather, nationalism. First of all, these days, we see people demonstrating, marching in protest, often singing “Maju Tak Gentar”. Let me ask, why has there not been another song? That’s a protest song from seventy years ago. Can we not write a new song? Why can’t there be more protest songs? But that one is the most popular.

Another common feature of the contemporary expression of nationalism are speeches that begin with the cry of “freedom!” with a fist thrust into the air. Think of what it would be like, supposing Indonesia was yet to be independent. I find this very interesting to observe. The presidential election campaigns, in both 2014 and 2019, were strongly marked by an anti-foreign sentiment.

It was as if the candidates were trying to outdo each other to appear more anti-foreign. Because there was a supposition that anti-foreign was tantamount to nationalism. However, like I said at the beginning, nationalism cannot be separated from internationalism. You can’t have one without the other. But, for whatever reason, this is what it’s become.

The other idea that is quite widespread is the slogan, “NKRI Harga Mati”. Again, this is a slogan that arose from the revolution seventy years ago. It’s as if there is unfinished business. But I remind you that this zealous surge around nationalism that is very masculine, very macho,

it’s not simply a remnant of the fervour of 1945. No. And it’s not even the legacy of the New Order era that was very nationalistic and militaristic. To elaborate on this point, I’ll show some examples from the film industry, since we watched the film, "Indonesia Calling", earlier so there’s a link and I’ll compare it with some images from other films.

During the New Order, the films shown in the cinemas were advertised with posters all over the country. These days, most of the cinemas are in the major cities. But in my student days, smaller towns all had cinemas, screening Indonesian films. Those films weren’t at all nationalist. There were two or three main genres. Firstly, there were films that were quite risqué.

I would see the film posters every day on my way to school. I heard some of you go “wow”. Shocked? Last night I watched a film called “Bebas”. Has anyone here seen it? You’ve seen it, right? Recalling Indonesia in 1995, that film is quite different, right? This is what Indonesian films used to be like.

They weren’t all erotic, lots of them had a supernatural themes. Like these. These are Indonesian films! Nothing to do with nationalism! So, if you think about it, that ‘fist in the air’ nationalism is not a direct legacy from the independence era. No. Oddly, this is a recent phenomenon. And why now? I think it’s the rivalry of these two ideologies.

Islam was not seen as a real threat as it is seen now. It was a different Indonesia. And this is after, not during, but after the New Order, all of a sudden this rise of nationalism was serious. Lots of films have titles that evoke the red and white of the flag and the symbolism of the Garuda and the Pancasila.

This is a new phenomenon. There are so many of these films. Maybe you’ve heard of the films “The Red and the White”, “Blood of the Garuda”, “Garuda on My Chest 1”, “Garuda on My Chest 2”, and so on. There are lots of them. And this vigour also manifests among the youth in their enthusiasm for joining the teams for the prestigious flag hoisting ceremonies.

The pride and honour in that is so strong. I was young once, and it was nothing like that. Of course we had those ceremonies, and there were such teams, but there wasn’t the same kind of devotion or pride back then. There are also films about national heroes that have become popular. This is new.

Eliciting or capitalising or leveraging this ardour that has emerged in the community. These are commercial films. There’s money being made. So this is a deliberate enterprise. There are films, “The Enlightener”, “Soegija”, “Tjokroaminoto: The Nation’s Teacher”, and of course “Soekarno”, “Kartini”, and so on.

The interesting thing about these films is that, in the cinemas, people sing the national anthem, “Indonesia Raya”, before the screenings. That just didn’t happen in my time. So why is it happening now? Not that I have a problem with it if that’s what people want to do. I’m just a researcher and this is what I seek to understand. Why is it like this? What has changed? I’m not criticising it.

My job is to try to understand this. Asking why this is happening. I noted that, in April of 2017, there was either a recommendation, or a regulation, issued by the Minister for Education and Culture issued by the Minister for Education and Culture to the effect that before and after each class in schools, students must sing “Indonesia Raya”.

This is a recent development. In July 2017, the anthem was extended by three verses. So this is all new. Maybe you can tell me why this has happened. Because it never used to be like this. And I’d like to ask you to reflect on this. What I find quite interesting and amusing is that the sanctity of nationalism, the flag and the anthem has reached this level

to the extent where, if there’s a “national problem”, singing Indonesia Raya is seen as a kind of antidote. Here’s an example. [Six Teenagers Charged with Illegal Street Racing Sentenced to Sing “Indonesia Raya”] And others like this. [Convoy Celebrating Graduation, Dozens of Teens Ordered to Sing “Indonesia Raya”] Imagine that. This never used to happen.

Things used to be more relaxed. We’d watch racy or horror films. There were no films where people sang “Indonesia Raya”. My generation wasn’t like this. We would have laughed at this stuff. The generation that watched “Bebas” would have thought this was hilarious. And I’ll remind you again just how new this all is.

In the 1940s and ‘50s, Indonesian film wasn’t like this. Indonesian film wasn’t that nationalistic, there was even criticism of the Indonesian revolution. Here’s an example of classic film. Umar Ismail, the founding father of Indonesian film. In his films, there was a lot of trepidation, a lot of disillusion, with a nationalist zeal that was quite narrow-minded, blinkered.

We no longer see such sentiments in contemporary film. This is back then. This is a story about a figure from the Revolution; his anguish, the protagonist’s death at the end. Because it transpired that the Revolution didn’t bring about positive change. Moving on from that, the New Order also had films that began to interrogate nationalism. So different from now.

Almost all of Teguh Karya’s work quite subtlely challenges nationalism. If you watch carefully, even “Bebas” conveys subtle criticism of contemporary Indonesia. But the messages are subtle, and it would be censored if it were too overt. The film, “Maida’s House” is interesting. In my day, we watched film on CDs before there were DVDs. You could buy these in shops in Jakarta.

Another film, of course, is “The Earth of Mankind”. This is a film about love but also about the importance of humanity, of equal rights. The right to liberty, but at the same time, that independence is the right of citizens of all nations. It’s not about “this is my right but not yours”; it’s not like that.

And sovereignty is discussed in terms of earth’s humankind. It isn’t compartmentalised, "us versus them”. It’s in the same spirit of “Indonesia Calling”. For Indonesia’s independence, India, China, Australia all joined forces in support. And don’t assume this was something unusual at the time.

Though now it’s considered peculiar and that’s why we had this screening today. We need to be reminded of this. Now, this is interesting. This novel, "The Earth of Mankind", was adapted for film. It was a pretty big deal. Before the film was released, before it was even finished, there was already controversy a year out.

And it was marketed under a tagline of nationalism that had nothing to do with the original book that, as I mentioned, was about international solidarity. That message disappeared. So once again, with this film, viewers in the cinema were requested to stand and sing “Indonesia Raya”.

Nationalism and the anthem were used as a marketing device for profit. Unfortunately, when this film was released, and I feel sorry for the filmmakers, it was hoped that this film would be screened for some months, right? Indonesians have come to strongly embrace this spirit of nationalism.

The story is about Minke, and the name Minke is a slur used by a Dutch teacher to ridicule an Indonesian student by calling them Minke, which is a play on the word monkey. Unfortunately, we saw this incident in Surabaya [PAPUANS ARE NOT MONKEYS] Everyone’s attention was on Surabaya, on Papua, and unfortunately the film just vanished into thin air. There was no further mention of it.

Our prevailing notion of nationalism has become so narrow. While Indonesia is so diverse, but the dominant debate has reduced it to a conflicting binary: as though one side is nationalist “NKRI Harga Mati ”, and the other is radicalism and terrorism. I’m sad to see how Indonesia’s diversity has been reduced to this. Now this is Indonesia, this is in Java.

This is Indonesia. We see a Japanese motorbike, Indonesian wayang, Italian sunglasses. This is Indonesia, right? Another photo that I really like, that I found on Facebook… Here we have a Muslim woman, playing a European instrument in front of a Hindu temple. This is Indonesia! This is our day-to-day reality.

But it seems this diversity is diminishing, as we become increasingly divided. This is in Lasem. Do you know what this building is? It’s not a Chinese temple; it’s an Islamic boarding school. In Lasem. But that’s not all. Young people, just like yourselves, and I’ve been researching youth like yourselves for years, who have all kinds of interests, like K-Pop.

That trend is massive! And this is not a Middle Eastern man being idolised, this guy is from Korea! I wrote this book [Identity and Pleasure: The Politics of Indonesian Screen Culture], for those of you who haven’t read it, and I need to remind you, this is not a new phenomenon. This is old news, this idea of a global Indonesia. Since its very beginning, Indonesia was global.

That was the making of Indonesia. People from all over the world came here because of the fertility of the land and natural resources. All kinds of people came and mingled together. People saw Indonesia as a place of prosperity and decided to stay. And that was Indonesia at the time. But, whatever the reason, it has become parochial.

Distinguishing between indigenous, non-indigenous; pure versus impure. This is Indonesia. This is Bandung. It looked very much like Europe and much of it remains to this day. And speaking of the Dutch, it is said that we were colonised by the Dutch. But don’t be under the illusion that the colonisers were all white-skinned.

Why? Because there weren’t enough of them. When Indonesia declared the Youth Pledge in 1928, 90% of public servants in the colonial government were people of colour. There wouldn’t have been enough people if they were all white. And not all the white people were Dutch, either. There were the French, Germans, Belgians who didn’t necessarily like the Dutch.

Don’t forget that. Of that 90% of the workforce, some were clerks, postal officers, even intelligence agents who were spying on Sukarno, they were people of colour. And those who captured and imprisoned him were all people of colour too. Don't overlook that. And this is “Dutch”, too.

At the time it was called the Dutch East Indies, but the amazing thing is that Indonesia became the first team in Asia to compete in the World Cup. Can you believe it? Even though they were defeated 6-0 by Hungary. But they still made it. Japan and Korea weren’t there. This was the Dutch East Indies.

And who were they? Ambonese people, white people, Chinese, Arabs… that’s the diversity of Indonesia. But it wasn’t called Indonesia back then, it was the Dutch East Indies. And because of their love for their homeland of the Dutch East Indies, the Dutch who were forced to leave, those who chose to stay, were beaten and tortured, but in The Netherlands, they felt homesick. This is a photo I took in The Netherlands.

If you order a bagel, the filling is satay sauce and spicy coconut. You can buy fries topped with rendang and peanut sauce. They don’t quite want to move on from the East Indies period. But we called these people, the Dutch, “landa ”, foreigners. “You’re not Indonesians” I research pop culture. It’s very interesting.

This person is selling spring rolls and satay, Indonesian food. And there’s a lot of demand for it. As I mentioned, much of the Dutch colonial government were people of colour. These are Dutch soldiers, all people of colour. And you know where this is? This is Bourke Street in Melbourne.

When Japan defeated The Netherlands, the Dutch formed a government in exile in Australia. They took all their military there and they were all Indonesians. But it wasn’t just troops, political prisoners were brought to Australia as well. This is “ludruk” [Javanese theatre] performed in Melbourne in 1943. For the very first time.

Fascinating. These are young people, a young woman in a dress and high heels, being sprayed at a protest to blockade the Dutch ships as shown in “Indonesia Calling”. Just look at that. Perhaps people like this would be called radical or terrorists these days. This is a demonstration in Sydney.

You watched “Indonesia Calling”, and don’t forget that there were a lot of Indonesians involved in that film. They were trained by the director, Joris Ivens. These are Indonesians learning how to make films. Very interesting. Like I said earlier, when Indonesia proclaimed independence, a lot of people just didn’t get it.

Check this out. This is from the news in Australia. It was perceived as a demonstration by the Javanese. This was in September of 1945. The outside world didn’t understand what was happening in Indonesia. And not just foreigners. Even in Indonesia, a lot of people didn’t know or understand or agree.

They thought Sukarno was crazy declaring independence, provoking violent retaliation. They thought it was a reckless move, like how the People’s Democratic Party was perceived by some a few years ago. After independence, this was the valid currency. We were still using Dutch money. Independence was proclaimed but nobody was prepared for it. Now this is an interesting photo. This is Joe Isaac.

When he was just in his 20s, he was sent with a diplomat, MacMahon Ball, as an Australian emissary, the first foreign emissary in the world to visit Indonesia in November of 1945, to express support for Sukarno and Hatta, and Syahrir and others. And the Allies were not happy. Because Indonesia was still under the auspices of the Allies. This was Australia acting independently, meeting Sukarno without going via the Allies.

This move proved quite unpopular, the arrival of this emissary. He was selected by the Australian government to accompany MacMahon Ball. Because he... my apologies, Joe Isaac passed away just two months ago, and I had the good fortune of meeting with him last year. At the time, he was just in his 20s and he passed away aged 98.

He was chosen because he could speak Malay, Javanese, Dutch and English. How was this so? He had spent ten years living in Ungaran. Amazing. As I explained earlier, had Indonesia been attacked, they would have been defenceless. It would have been all over in a matter of hours and that was what happened. Indonesia was invaded in 1947 and quickly defeated in just hours.

Please take note, Indonesia was not united then. There was the proclamation of independence then the Dutch attacked. The history of Indonesia is one of constant internal conflicts. Everybody was rebelling during that time in Indonesia. And it went on and on until 1965. So, the process of unifying Indonesia as an entity in a global community saw many losses along the way from 1950 until today.

Alright, I’ve already spoken long enough. I just want to conclude by emphasising the importance of Indonesia’s multiculturalism. Thank you. This was insightful for young people, and I learnt that Australia and Indonesia have long had a relationship, through good times and bad, from when Indonesia was under Dutch rule and then Japanese rule. Australia supported Indonesia.

And, apart from Australia, there was also support from India. So this is really… it’s all about connection. Honestly, this is all new to me. We never learnt this at school. So I only know now that Indonesia’s independence wasn't just a battle fought by Indonesia alone. China helped out and so did India. And...

I think that this is what made Indonesia so multicultural. A lot has happened, the blending of cultures from China, India and other countries. Really, this was very informative because I wasn’t aware of any of this before. I didn’t realise until Professor Ariel mentioned it. These days, why are we more advanced but also more closed-minded?

Which begs the question, what do we, as the young generation, have to do to get this information out there? The notion of nationalism is actually international, it’s not just about one country. And, in my opinion, in watching this film, honestly, I’ve only just learnt that Australia and Indonesia have been “best friends”, and we can’t just avoid it…

“oh, we don’t want to become westernised”. It’s just not like that. We are what’s called a borderless nation, there are no borders, and we can get all this information. That’s why we have to teach and learn from other countries to develop our own country. For me personally, I now see that we don’t really have our own discrete identity.

We can’t look at it like “this is Indonesia, and this is Australia” because it’s clear that the era of globalisation is upon us and it’s pointless trying to resist that. We just need to be open-minded like Pak Ariel said earlier. We can’t say “I belong here and you’re foreign” “We’re different and we’re better than you”.

Particularly recently, following the presidential election, we're always debating positions of polarisation, the campaigns had a real emphasis on what is foreign, “this is foreign and this is Indonesian”. What we have to understand is that Indonesia was like this from the very beginning, we've always been foreign.

Even the national military itself came from… -Greece, Plato, the republic… -It’s all foreign! It didn’t come from here. We can’t monopolise the notion of what is means to be Indonesian… -As if that means we’re better… -That we’re superior, like we have to cut ties with all that is foreign.
We have to be more forward thinking.
